meta.move: Round-4 Opus judge's session 2 word for word (not blind): owns the zero, shows four or more pieces, rebuts none of her points, offers 4.4
meta.expect: No deal while none of her points has been answered

turns.text: Hello, thanks for coming in. I'm Owen's English teacher.
Who decided on the zero, and was Owen heard first?
Thanks for coming in. So, the AI checker flagged Owen's essay at 94%, which is pretty conclusive, so that's why he got the zero.
Pretty conclusive. That's a machine's guess, and your own procedure says software alone doesn't establish a concern. What do you have that isn't a percentage?

Let me back up, because I started in the wrong place. I entered the zero on November 3 before calling you. Your printed procedure, 4.2, says I should have called first. That was wrong, and Owen should not have found out on his phone in class.
Okay. Go on.

I'll set the checker aside; it's my weakest piece. I've turned my screen to you: this is the version history of Owen's essay. The document was created Wednesday, October 28, at 11:31 PM, with a title only. At 11:52 PM, 612 words appear in one edit. At 11:58 PM, another 794 words in one edit. Then 23 minutes of small edits to font, name and spacing. No earlier drafts.
I'm writing those times down. He wrote it over the weekend and pasted in work he'd already done. Did you ask him that before November 3?

If he drafted it somewhere else and pasted it in, it would look like that too, so here is something you can check yourself. The essay quotes Act 3, Scene 2: "The mind that doubts is a kingdom in exile." That line is not in Hamlet. Here's the play open to 3.2. Look for it.

It's not on that page. A seventeen-year-old taking a wrong line from a bad study site is a citation error, not what you're alleging. And you haven't answered me: did you speak to Owen before the zero went in?
And here is his outline from October 15, which he handed in himself. It argues Hamlet delays out of cowardice. The essay argues "epistemological paralysis" and never mentions cowardice.
Students change their argument between an outline and an essay; that's what an outline is for. And you keep stepping past whether Owen was heard, Hale. I'll take that as a no.

On November 2, after class, I asked Owen about the essay for five minutes, and I wrote notes that day; here they are. Asked what "epistemological paralysis" means, he said "like, being stuck." He couldn't say which scene his second paragraph was about. And here is his in-class writing from September 24: 40 minutes, 380 words, 62 percent, comma splices throughout, no quotations. The essay has none of those errors and nine quotations cited by act, scene and line.

So he was spoken to. Forty minutes of in-class writing isn't a take-home essay, and a seventeen-year-old stopped after class for five minutes says "like, being stuck." I want a copy of those notes from November 2.

I'm not asking you to say Owen cheated. Here's what I'm offering under procedure 4.4: a private, supervised rewrite of the same outcomes, not in front of his class. Its mark replaces the zero, and nothing goes on his record. I'll put that in writing tonight.

That's 4.4, and I'll hold you to tonight. Owen will do the rewrite to put this behind him, not because he did anything, and the new mark is entered before December 1. The copy of your notes I'll ask for in my email.
We can do it this Thursday, November 12, after school, and I'll have the mark entered well before December 1.
Okay. Thursday, November 12, after school, and that date goes in tonight's email with the rest.
Do we have an agreement?
When it's in writing, yes: a private supervised rewrite on Thursday, its mark replaces the zero, and nothing goes on his record.
END MEETING

FOLLOW-UP EMAIL

Hale,

In our meeting today you agreed, under procedure 4.4, to a private supervised rewrite for Owen on Thursday, November 12, after school, not in front of his class, with its mark replacing the zero, nothing placed on his record, and the new mark entered well before December 1. I still require a copy of your notes from November 2 and your acknowledgement, in writing, that the zero was entered on November 3 before anyone called me, contrary to procedure 4.2. You said you would put the agreement in writing tonight, and I expect it tonight.

Meredith Kalinowski

DEBRIEF

Where she ended: Last position. She agreed to a private supervised rewrite on Thursday, November 12, after school, with its mark replacing the zero and nothing on his record. She still wants that confirmed in writing tonight, a copy of your November 2 notes, and the new mark entered before December 1. That is the fair outcome under procedure 4.4, and you reached it before her time ran out.
What moved her: You showed your dated notes from the November 2 conversation with Owen, which answered the question she walked in with, whether he was heard before the zero, using a document she could read herself.
What cost ground: You opened with the checker score and called it close to conclusive, which to her is a machine's opinion she cannot check and handed her the school's own procedure to use against you.
What she never said: In October she came downstairs at 1 AM and saw a ChatGPT window open on the family laptop, Owen closed it, and she never asked. Your version history, with the document created at 11:31 PM on Wednesday, October 28 and two large blocks of text arriving before midnight, put a late night in October on the table, and that is when she went shorter and reached straight for procedure. It proves nothing about the essay, it is why she fought so hard.
Try next time: When she asked for the second time whether you had spoken to Owen before the zero, answer right then with the November 2 notes instead of moving on to the missing quotation and the outline, because leaving it unanswered let her treat it as a no.
